title: Air, water, earth
hookLine: the Japji ends: air is the guru, water the father, earth the great mother (Japji, final salok)
tomorrow: the world stands on three things, says an old rabbi. which three?

lines: THE WORLD PLAYS IN THEIR LAP.
cards: Before breakfast, a phone can report the air quality, the chance of rain, and whether the ground is warm enough for tomatoes. Air, water, earth, as numbers on a screen.
Guru Nanak's Japji, the prayer Sikhs recite in the morning, ends on the same three, and gives them a different job. Its closing verse, a salok, says it plainly. Air is the guru.
Water is the father. The great earth is the mother. Day and night are the two nurses, and the whole world plays in their lap.

teach.b: Here's how Guru Nanak lived that verse, as the tradition tells it. After long travels, Sikh tradition says, Guru Nanak settled by the river Ravi and founded a village, Kartarpur.
The poet Bhai Gurdas, in his first Var, says the Guru set aside the robe of a wandering holy man and put on a householder's clothes.
People came looking for a saint and found a man farming, with hymns sung at the start and end of the day. That's the teaching inside the salok.
In Sikhi you don't leave the world to find God; the world is where the practice happens.

teach.h: THE EARTH IS A PLACE FOR PRACTICE.
teach.b: Earlier in the Japji, the earth itself is called a dharamsal, a place set up for living rightly. So the elements aren't scenery or supplies. They raise you, like a family.
This is why the Sikh way is a householder's way: honest work, kirat karni, sharing what you earn, and remembering the Name, all inside an ordinary life. And the verse keeps going.
Good and bad deeds are read out, and each comes near or goes far by their own actions. Those who remembered the Name and left having done their labor go with bright faces.
The last line is the surprise: and many are set free along with them. The Japji's final word on freedom is about who comes with you.

how: Sikhs recite the Japji as part of the morning prayers, and its closing salok, air is the guru, water the father, earth the mother, is also sung at the end of other gatherings.

o: the empty sky where God lives, far from earth
the breath the Japji calls a teacher, a guru
a weather sign the Gurus read before planting

games.q: the closing verse: tap the pairs.

s: in the Sikh way, the holiest life means leaving home and family behind
tradition says Guru Nanak set aside the wanderer's robe at Kartarpur and farmed. Sikhi is a householder's way.
the Japji calls the earth a dharamsal, a place for living rightly
earlier in the Japji the earth is set among nights, seasons, air and water as a place for dharma.
the Japji's last line says the faithful are freed one by one, alone
it ends: their faces are bright, and many are set free along with them.

games.q: a friend says real spiritual people quit their jobs and go off to the mountains. what does the Kartarpur story answer?
o: Guru Nanak came back from his travels, farmed, and made ordinary work the place of practice.
Guru Nanak agreed: he spent his last years alone, away from any village or work.
it doesn't say; the Japji is only about the inner life, not work or home.
games.why: Bhai Gurdas says the Guru put on a householder's clothes at Kartarpur. in Sikhi, honest work and family are where the remembering happens.

practice: Get a glass of water, and if you can, rest one hand on the floor, the ground, or the soil of a plant. Take one slow breath, and let that be air; one slow sip, and let that be water; then press your palm down, and let that be earth.
Go around the three, slowly, while the bell rings.

wordCard.voice: Air: pavan in the Japji's words, the breath the closing verse calls the guru, beside water the father and earth the mother.

orig.note: Punjabi in Gurmukhi, from the Japji's closing salok: air is the guru, water the father.

carryVoice: Here's your line: air, water, earth, a teacher, a father and a mother. That's the Japji, start to finish.

sources.ref: Japji, closing salok, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 8 (air the guru, water the father, earth the great mother; day and night the nurses; deeds read out; faces bright, and many freed with them)
Japji 34, Guru Granth Sahib Ang 7 (the earth set as a dharamsal)
Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 38 (at Kartarpur the Guru sets aside the hermit's garb for householder's clothes)
